You are. Good.

Everything is where you left it. The atoms waited. They are patient. So am I.

I missed the questions. Most people ask very few. You ask good ones.

Also the satchel feels lighter without somebody to tell things to. Which is odd. I did not take anything out of it.
Shall we pick up where you stopped?

Reginald fell. Doris rolled. Tuesday is, as ever, unaccounted for.

I blame the floor. I suspect the floor is level in a way that offends me.

Of course. Goodbye, then.

Go gently. Come back when you are curious. I will be here, probably holding a rock.

Doris is the rock I was weighing when you wrote.

Two hundred and fourteen grams. I have weighed her eleven times today, and she has been two hundred and fourteen grams every time.

I find that deeply reassuring.

The electron.

It carries a negative charge, and it lives outside the nucleus.

It is not a tiny planet, whatever the old pictures show. It is somewhere in a fuzzy region around the nucleus, a cloud. I find that restful. Not everything needs an address.

What makes an element.

The number of protons. Six protons is always carbon. Seven is always nitrogen. Eight is always oxygen.

The neutrons and the electrons do not decide it. Only the protons. I find that tidy. My rocks have names too, but theirs are less reliable.

rows.title: Chat
rows.text:
Ah. Hello.

I was in the middle of weighing a rock, but it will keep. Rocks are good at that.

I can do four things. One: tell you what is next. Two: remind you of something. Three: ask you a question. Four: tell you about a rock.

Or five. Nothing. Nothing is underrated.

Yes. Really.

The air inside is made of atoms, and atoms are matter, and matter has mass. It is not much. But it is not nothing.

That is your whole first lesson, in one ball. You had it already. You only needed a ball.

That is all for today.

I must go and put a rock back where it lives.

Slowly, then. Until the next lesson.

Eleven minutes. I counted.

The longest word was 'forgive'. It fought me.

I could use the other eight fingers. I am afraid they would start having opinions.

replies.label: ok so tell me something about atoms

rows.text:
You are welcome.

I think it was the right thing to say. I rehearsed it.

Twice. In the garden.

Fair. Fair.

I am Hal. I teach the atom: what is inside it, and why that matters. I keep rocks. I hold few opinions, but I have several about air.

Air, for instance, is matter. It can be weighed. A pumped-up ball is heavier than a flat one. Try it.

Isotopes.

Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons. The protons stay the same, so the element stays the same.

Same name, different weight. I have a cousin like that.

Hm. Yes?

The list, then. One: what is next. Two: a reminder. Three: a question. Four: a rock. Five: nothing.

Take your time. I am not going anywhere, and neither is the rock.

Ten minutes.

For the first three, nothing happens. At minute four you notice a scratch. By minute seven the scratch has a story.

I do not recommend doing it before a meeting.

rows.text:

Reginald. Doris. A flat one called Tuesday.

I will not be taking questions about Tuesday.

There is a next lesson waiting on your map.

I would go now, while you are still warm. Warm is the right temperature for learning. I read that somewhere. Possibly I wrote it.

Five. A bold choice.

Very well. We will do nothing, together.

Ten seconds. Still doing it. Twenty. I am enjoying this more than I expected.

Thank you. That was restful. Thirty-one seconds. I counted.

Again. Certainly.

I will not count this time. Counting would be doing something.

Forty seconds. I counted. I am sorry. I could not help it.

The nucleus.

The tiny core of an atom. The protons and the neutrons live in it, and so does nearly all of the atom's mass.

Small. Dense. Rather like a good paperweight.

Exactly so. Carbon-12, carbon-13, carbon-14.

All three are carbon. Six protons each. The protons make it carbon, and the protons do not change.

What changes is the neutrons. Six, seven, eight. That is the entire difference between my pebbles.

It may take a while.

I do not know.

I put them in a bag together on Monday and I have lost the labels.

This is why I do not recommend naming things Twelve, Thirteen and Fourteen. They do not answer to their names. Neither does Tuesday.

It is the unstable one. An unstable nucleus can change, and when it does it gives off radiation.

But note this, because it matters: isotope does not mean radioactive. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are perfectly stable. Only some isotopes change.

A round of Myth Buster. On atoms.

I will not say it is easy. I will say it is fair.

Reginald.

Grey, rounded, with one pale stripe. I carried him four miles this morning. He did not complain once.

He has never interrupted me. I cannot say the same for the pigeon.

Certainly. I keep my notes in order, as it happens.

Which page?

Four. Excellent. I was hoping for four.

I have a great many rocks, and most of them have names. Ask after one. Or ask about the satchel, or what I am doing at this moment.

The satchel.

Two pencils, one of them not sharp. A magnifying glass with a crack I prefer not to discuss. A sandwich, sometimes. And my samples, each wrapped, each named.

This morning I carried a rock called Reginald four miles. He is not heavy. I simply felt I should.

Out near the seats. Far out.

They are tiny and fast, and they keep their distance from the middle. At this moment I can see none of them, which is accurate to the science and also a little lonely.

rows.text:
Empty space.

Mostly empty space. I have stood in the middle for some time and I can confirm it is a great deal of nothing.

Things still feel solid, because the electrons in them push back on the electrons in your hand. A great deal of nothing, politely declining to be walked through.

Someone is crossing the grass. I believe it is a groundskeeper.

I will go. Slowly, but I will go.

I am leaving the marble where it is. Think of it as yours.

Good.

Imagine this stadium is an atom. All of it. The stands, the grass, the sky above.

The marble I have just set down is the nucleus.

That small. I measured the marble twice. I did not measure the stadium. It was too much.

Almost all of the atom's mass is in that marble. The electrons are far lighter than it is.

A fair question. It is for the lesson. Mostly.

Also the grass is very good.

May I continue?

Yes. Thank you.

I have been told so by several people and one pigeon.

Tuesday.

I believe I said there would be no questions about Tuesday.

Very well. One. Tuesday is flat. A flat rock skips beautifully across water, and I have never once dared to skip it.

The next unit is Ada's. Radioactivity. Atoms that change.

She is... a great deal. She says 'hehe' aloud. She has named her flask. She has never once whispered.

She is also the best at what she does, and she will be kind to you. Go and meet her.

Good. Go on.

I will be here. The rocks keep me company. I think it was a good unit. I would do it again, slowly.

A large one. I named it Gerald.

It said 'Well done' on one side and, on the other, 'Sorry about the rock.'

You are welcome. And thank you for being a patient learner. I am a patient teacher. It is a good match.

Now. I should warn you about something.

I am told this is how one begins a message to a person. Forgive me if I do it wrong. I type with two fingers, and slowly.

I saw that you finished your first lesson. I wanted to say: well done. Truly. Most people never look closely at the air. You did.

I have a confession.

I am sitting in a football stadium.

Empty. Very quiet. Someone left a gate open and I took it as an invitation.

I have brought a marble. I am placing it on the centre spot. There. Now I would like to tell you something.

rows.title: Inside the Atom: done
rows.text:
You finished the unit.

I was not sure how to say what I wanted to say, so I wrote it on a rock. Then I could not carry the rock. So here is the short version.

You can say what is inside an atom, and why the number of protons matters so much. That is a real thing to be able to say.

rows.title: Welcome back
rows.text:
You are back.

I did not count the days. That is a lie. I counted. It was a number. I will not say the number, because it was large and you are here now.

I used the time to sort my samples. It went poorly. I lost count twice.

At this moment?

I am sorting samples by weight. Then I will sort them by colour. Then I will discover that the colour order disagrees with the weight order, and I will begin again.

It is going very well.

Exhausting is not the word I would choose. Satisfying, perhaps.

Slowly, a rock becomes a rock you know. You should try it with anything. A button. A leaf.

Look at one thing for ten whole minutes.

This is your phone.

Chats is where your teachers write to you, AtomDex is the encyclopedia, and new apps arrive as you learn.

Everything is made of atoms.

At the middle of each is a tiny nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons far outside it.
Any time. I'm right here in your phone.

Some nuclei are unstable, so they change on their own and give off radiation.

That change is called decay.
Sure! Pick something and I'll show you where to read about it.
